questions.q: A user says "the app is slow today". Which signal tells you where the time of one slow request went?
questions.explain: A trace is the story of one request, split into timed steps (spans). Metrics tell you how much and how fast over time, and logs tell you what happened in detail.

questions.q: What does createObservability(...) give you?
questions.explain: One object holds all three signals and the propagation that links them. The exporters are the parts that send the data somewhere, by default to the console.
options: An HTTP server with logging built in
A logger, a metrics registry, a tracer and a propagation manager, plus the exporters that send the data
A dashboard website for your metrics

questions.q: Which createObservability call follows the lesson's advice for a real service?
questions.explain: The lesson says: always pass redaction: {}, so secret fields such as password are hidden with the default field list. Being explicit keeps you safe whatever the default is. The service name tells the monitoring system which service sent the data.

questions.q: This project prints log records with its own exporter. What does it print?
questions.explain: With redaction: {}, fields with secret names like password are replaced before any exporter sees them. In this logger the metadata is called context.

questions.q: Why must you call await obs.shutdown() before the process exits?
questions.explain: Batching is much cheaper than one network call per record, but records wait in memory until the next batch. shutdown() sends the rest, which are often the most important last records.
options: It resets all counters to zero
Exporters send in batches; shutdown sends what is left and closes them, or the last records are lost
It deletes the logs from the console

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The exporter works in batches, so the log record waits in memory. It is sent when shutdown() flushes the batch, after "still running" was printed.

questions.q: You want to track how many jobs are waiting in the email queue right now. Which kind of metric fits?
questions.explain: A counter only goes up (requests served, tasks created). The queue length goes up when jobs arrive and down when they are done, which is what a gauge is for.
options: A counter, because jobs are counted
A gauge, because the number goes up and down
A histogram, because it gives percentiles
A log line for every job

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A metric is identified by its name and its labels. The first two calls reach the same counter (1 + 2 = 3). The one with { priority: "high" } is a different series.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A counter can never decrease, so increment(-1) throws a MetricValueError and the value stays 5. Something that goes up and down, like open tasks, needs a gauge.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A gauge can be set, lowered and raised: 12, then 10, then 11.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Four measurements add up to 1000, so the mean is 250 ms, although three of the four requests took 30 ms or less. That is why you should not judge speed by the mean.

questions.q: Nine requests took 12 to 40 ms and one took 900 ms. The mean is 111.7 ms. What should you alert on?
questions.explain: The mean of 111.7 ms describes none of the real requests. A percentile says "95% were faster than this", which matches what users experience. Alert on p95 or p99, never on the mean.
options: The mean, because it includes every request
A percentile such as p95 or p99, because it shows what users actually feel

questions.q: A histogram reports p50: 23. What does that mean?
questions.explain: p50 is the 50th percentile, also called the median: half the values are below it. The histogram estimates it from buckets, so it is close but not exact.
options: About half of the requests were faster than 23 ms

questions.q: Why should you not add { userId } as a label on http.requests?
questions.explain: Every different set of labels is a separate series. A few values like route and status are fine. Ids belong in logs and traces, never in metric labels.
options: The counter would count each request twice
Each user becomes a separate series stored forever; a million users means a million series (a cardinality explosion)
It would hide the user id from the logs

questions.q: Which label is a good idea on a tasks.created counter?
questions.explain: A priority has three possible values, so it makes three series at most. A title, an id or a time can take endless values, and each one would become a new series.
options: { priority } with the values low, medium and high

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each set of labels is one series, and asking again for the same labels returns the same counter. So there are two series: low with 3 and high with 1, in the order they were first created.

questions.q: The request wrapper labels metrics with the route. Which value should it pass for GET /tasks/7?
questions.explain: A real path contains an id, so every task would become a new series. The route template has one value for all tasks.
options: The full URL with the query string

questions.q: What is a span?
questions.explain: A trace is made of spans, one per step. Spans nest: a span started inside another becomes its child, and all spans of one trace share one trace id.
options: One step of a trace, with a name, a start, an end and attributes
A group of log lines with the same level

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: withSpan starts a span, runs your function, ends the span and gives back the function's result. So you can wrap a step without changing what it returns.

questions.q: This exporter prints each span's name and status. Spans are exported in the order they end. What does it print?
questions.explain: The error went up through both spans, so both are marked ERROR. The inner span ends first. The spans are printed last, because the exporter sends its batch at shutdown.
options:
failed: duplicate key
db.insert ERROR
POST /tasks ERROR

failed: duplicate key
db.insert ERROR
POST /tasks UNSET

failed: duplicate key
POST /tasks ERROR
db.insert ERROR

db.insert ERROR
POST /tasks ERROR
failed: duplicate key

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A span started while another is active becomes its child: it shares the trace id and points at the parent span id. Nobody passed the parent as a parameter; withSpan made it the active span.

questions.q: Which span kind marks the span that handles an incoming request?
questions.explain: SERVER is for handling a request that came in. When your service calls another system, that span is a CLIENT span.

questions.q: How does a nested span or a log line know the current trace id without a parameter?
questions.explain: AsyncLocalStorage stores a value for one chain of async calls, through any number of awaits. Two requests running at the same time each see their own value; a global variable would mix them up.
options: It reads a global variable that each request overwrites
The context is kept in an AsyncLocalStorage, which follows one chain of async calls
The trace id is stored in the log message text
It asks the client for the trace id again

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Inside propagation.run, every function can read the context, even without a parameter. Outside a run there is no context, so the fallback "none" is printed.

questions.q: Two requests run at the same time, and ada's takes longer. What does this print?
questions.explain: linus finishes first, but each call still sees its own request: AsyncLocalStorage keeps one value per async chain. A shared global variable would have given both the last request.
options:
linus sees req-2
ada sees req-1

ada sees req-1
linus sees req-2

linus sees req-2
ada sees req-2

linus sees undefined
ada sees undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every log record written inside a propagation context gets its trace id automatically. The line outside any run has no trace id.
options:
tasks loaded trace=4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736
outside any request trace=-

tasks loaded trace=-
outside any request trace=-

tasks loaded trace=4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736
outside any request trace=4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736

questions.q: A user reports an error. What does the lesson suggest putting in your error responses so you can find everything about that request?
questions.explain: The trace id is on every log line and span of the request, so it works as a correlation id. It reveals nothing about your system, unlike a stack trace or SQL.
options: The trace id, for example as a traceId field
The server's hostname and memory use

questions.q: What does the W3C traceparent header contain?
questions.explain: The caller sends its trace id and current span id, plus flags that say whether it kept (sampled) the trace. The receiver starts its spans as children of that span.
options: The user id and their role
The full list of spans of the caller
A signed token that proves who the caller is

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The header has four parts separated by dashes: version 00, the 32-character trace id, the 16-character span id and the flags. The flags 01 become the number 1: the caller kept the trace.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: parseTraceparent checks the header and returns undefined for anything malformed or missing. The server then simply starts a fresh trace instead of failing.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The flags 00 mean the caller did not keep the trace, so traceFlags is 0. Formatting the parsed context gives back the same header.

questions.q: A client sends traceparent and x-user-role: admin. The Task API joins the trace. What about the role?
questions.explain: Joining a trace only links spans; at worst, a client makes its request appear inside someone else's trace. A role decides what the caller may do, so it must never come from a header the client can type.
options: Trust it too: the client already sent a valid traceparent
Trust it only when the traceparent's flags are 01
Never trust it: roles come from your own authentication, such as a verified session or token
Trust it for read requests only

questions.q: What may an incoming traceparent header decide in your service?
questions.explain: The header comes from outside, so it is untrusted. Give it only as much power as it can safely have: linking spans. It must never decide what a caller may do.
options: Which tenant's data the request can read
Only how spans are linked into a trace (and, with a parent-based sampler, whether the trace is kept)
Whether the request skips rate limiting
Which log level the request uses

questions.q: A handler throws new Error("report service unreachable"). What does the instrumented Task API send to the client?
questions.explain: Internal error messages can reveal how your system works. The wrapper records the error on the span and logs it, and gives the client only a safe message.
options: 500 with the stack trace, so the client can report it
A plain 500 with { error: "Internal Server Error" }; the message stays in the log and on the span
200 with an empty list, so the client does not notice

questions.q: During an incident, in which order does the lesson suggest using the three signals?
questions.explain: An alert on a metric (like 5xx rate or p95) tells you there is a problem. A log search finds the error and its trace id. The trace with that id shows which step failed or was slow.
options: Metrics show something is wrong, logs show what went wrong, the trace shows where
Logs only; the others are for later

questions.q: What should change about exporters before you deploy?
questions.explain: The console exporters are for development. In production you implement the SpanExporter, LogExporter and MetricExporter interfaces (or install a package that does) and send the data to a collector.
options: Nothing: the console exporters are made for production
Pass real exporters that send to your monitoring system, usually an OpenTelemetry collector
Remove all exporters, so nothing slows the service
Write every record to a local file

questions.q: With sampling, when is the "keep this trace or not" decision made?
questions.explain: Deciding once per trace means you never get half a trace. A parent-based sampler also follows the caller's decision from the traceparent flags.
options: Once, for the first span of a trace; every child span follows it
At shutdown, based on how slow the trace was
By the client for every request

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A parent-based sampler follows the caller when there is one. Flags 01 mean the caller kept the trace, so this span records; 00 means it did not. The 10% root sampler is only used for traces that start here.

questions.q: You sample 10% of traces. What happens to the http.requests counter?
questions.explain: Sampling keeps a share of the traces, which are the expensive part. Metrics are cheap numbers and still count every request.
options: It also counts only 10% of requests
It still counts every request: metrics are not sampled
It stops counting until sampling is turned off
It counts only the requests whose trace was kept

questions.q: Where should the Task API call await obs.shutdown()?
questions.explain: Stop accepting requests first, so the last requests can still be recorded. Then shut down observability, which sends the remaining batches.
options: At the start of every request
In the SIGTERM handler, after the HTTP server has stopped
Before the HTTP server stops, so no request is traced
Never: the process exit sends the data

questions.q: In unit tests you use createNoopObservability(). What does this print?
questions.explain: The no-op object has the same methods as the real one, so your code runs unchanged, but it records nothing. The counter stays 0.
options: TypeError: obs.metrics.counter is not a function

questions.q: Finish summary(durations): return an object with the mean (the average) and the median, the middle value after sorting (use the element at index Math.floor((n - 1) / 2)). The program should print { mean: 111.7, median: 22 }.
questions.explain: Sort numbers with (a, b) => a - b; the default sort compares text. One slow request pulls the mean up to 111.7 ms, while the median shows that a typical request takes about 22 ms.

questions.q: Finish isValidTraceparent(header): return true only for a string of the form 00- + 32 lower-case hex characters + - + 16 lower-case hex characters + -01 or -00. Anything else, including undefined, is false. The program should print true false false false.
questions.explain: Anchor the pattern with ^ and $, so extra text at the end is rejected. The header comes from the client, so check it strictly and treat anything else as "no parent".

questions.q:
Finish toTraceparent(span): build the header 00-<traceId>-<spanId>-<flags>, where the flags are 01 when span.sampled is true and 00 otherwise. The program should print:

00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-00
questions.explain: The caller sends its current span id, so the receiver's spans become its children. The last part tells the receiver whether the caller kept the trace.

questions.q: Finish metricLabels(request, status) so it returns only safe labels: the route template and the status as a string. Never the path, the user id or the task id. The program should print { route: '/tasks/:id', status: '200' }.
questions.explain: Each different label set is a stored series. The template /tasks/:id has one value for every task, and a status has a handful. The path and the user id would make one series per task or per user.

questions.q:
A metric is identified by its name and its labels. Finish seriesKey(name, labels): sort the label names, and return name{key=value,key=value}. The same labels in a different order must give the same key. The program should print:

http.requests{route=/tasks,status=200}
true
questions.explain: Sorting the keys makes the key independent of the order you wrote the labels in. That is how asking again for the same name and labels can return the same counter.

questions.q: Finish slowestChild(spans, rootName): find the root span by name, then return the name of its child (a span whose parent is the root's id) with the largest ms. The program should print db.insert.
questions.explain: Spans point at their parent's id, which is how a trace becomes a tree. The child with the most time is where optimizing pays off.

questions.q: Finish errorBody(error, traceId) for a 500 response: return { error: "Internal Server Error", traceId }. Do not include the error's message or stack. The program should print {"error":"Internal Server Error","traceId":"4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736"}.
questions.explain: The message reveals an internal address, so it goes only to the log and the span. The trace id lets the user report the problem, and lets you find every log line and span of that request.
